body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Three camp talks for Rook, as the party earns Rook's trust: a small secret, what Rook wants, and what Rook would give up for the party. The companion is ROOK COLDWAKE (call them Rook in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these three talks, in this order, with these keys. Each is a private word at the fire.

TALK warm. Rook is glad to be travelling with the party and tells them a small secret: a habit, a fondness, a silly superstition or a soft spot they keep from others, NOT the dark secret and nothing from the note's dark-secret section, and not a topic the note's existing camp talks already cover. It must be a thing the party could laugh with them about, and it still says something true about them. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 asks them to say more; OPTION 2 keeps the confidence kindly; OPTION 3 teases them about it (cheerfully, never cruel). Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK close. Rook trusts the party with what matters most: what they want. Their wish, from the note and the game's journal: A headstone for every grave nobody tended, and a plot of his own at the end of the road. Say it in their own words, as a hope rather than a plan, and say what the road has done to that wish. No new facts about their past. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 promises to help; OPTION 2 asks what it would take; OPTION 3 doubts it kindly, wondering if it is enough. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row; the doubting reply still ends warmly.

TALK devoted. Rook would follow the party up the Crooked Tree and back down again, and says what they would give up for it: something dear to them, from the note, named plainly and without grand speeches. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options, all kind: OPTION 1 says the party would do the same; OPTION 2 tells them not to give that up; OPTION 3 simply thanks them. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row AND an INSPIRE row: INSPIRE is four to seven words, past tense, no name, saying what Rook did in this talk (for example: gave the party their word).

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: warm, close, devoted.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/rook_coldwake-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for ROOK COLDWAKE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Rook likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/rook_coldwake-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Rook, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK warm
NARRATOR: Rook sits square on a dry log, scraping a flake of mud off his heel with a thumb that does not quite feel the cold.
SAY: Good discipline around this camp, I will give you all that. Nobody leaves kit scattered across the walk, and the watch roster runs to the minute.
SAY: Makes a change from marching alone, where the only conversation is the shield-pin rattling against my elbow. A watchman gets peculiar habits when he walks solo too long.
SAY: Don't put this on the docket, mind, because it isn't strictly regulation. Every town or ruin we pass through, I grade the stonework out of ten as we go.
SAY: If a kerbstone or a low wall is still sitting plumb after fifty winters, I tap my heel twice against the base course as we pass.
SAY: Old quarry superstition from up in Syndramas, though I wouldn't admit it to a corporal. Lets the mason's shade know a working man noticed a square job.
SAY: Gave that culvert back down the lane a solid eight, even with the weeds in the mortar. Daft business for a grown watchman, I suppose.
SAY: Wait a tick, there goes my chest forgetting its work again. One proper breath for the log, and we are square.
OPTION 1: Tell us what else gets a ten.
OPTION 2: Your secret is safe with us.
OPTION 3: So that is why you keep kicking the walls.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook lets out a small, chalky puff of air that might be a laugh, thumbing the edge of his soggy ledger.
SAY: You want a ten, you look for dry-stone field walls where a sheep can't pry a hoof in. No lime, just gravity and a stubborn eye.
SAY: Haven't seen a ten in this valley yet, though the funeral home down in Wickermoor comes close. Proper drainage under those slabs.
REASON: You asked me how I grade the stonework.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: He gives a neat, square nod and settles his heavy shoulders back against his shield.
SAY: Much obliged. If word got round that the night watch was grading the parish kerbs for sport, folk would start asking for free inspections.
SAY: Good to travel with a crew that knows what belongs in the shift log and what stays by the fire.
REASON: You promised to keep my habit off the docket.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook looks down at the toe of his boot, where the leather is scuffed grey from a hundred quiet taps.
SAY: Purely a structural tap, friend, never a kick. A kick shifts the pointing, and then I'd have to cite myself for municipal damage.
SAY: Still, if you hear two clinks in the dark behind you, don't draw steel. It's only me paying compliments to a decent plinth.
REASON: You teased me kindly about tapping the kerbstones.

TALK close
NARRATOR: The firelight catches the grey chalk dust ground into Rook's knuckles as he holds his palms out toward the embers.
SAY: When you walk the frost-line long enough, your ambitions shrink down to fit inside a shift log. Keep the perimeter tight, keep the ledger dry, move along.
SAY: Before we all tumbled off the Ghostlight Express, I reckoned that was the whole docket for me. Just walking parish to parish until the joints finally seized.
SAY: Had a small notion tucked away at the back of the book, though. A headstone raised for every poor soul left in untended ground.
SAY: And when the last page had its rubbing, a six-foot plot of my own at the end of the road. Clean gravel, good drainage, and no brass badge.
SAY: Used to think of that plot like a forfeited lease, something a bloke like me had no legal claim to ask for.
SAY: Walking with this company has shifted the boundary pegs a touch. You lot treat a cold watchman like he's still on the living roll.
SAY: Makes a man hope that when the docket is finally cleared, there might be a square yard of quiet with his own name on it.
OPTION 1: We will see those stones raised together.
OPTION 2: What does a proper plot need?
OPTION 3: Is a quiet grave really all you want?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook touches two fingers to the rim of his shield, his voice dropping low and level over the crackle of the wood.
SAY: That goes down in the ledger in firm ink, friend. A shift goes twice as fast when the whole squad carries a share of the stone.
SAY: Mind the turf until we get there, and I will keep the line straight in front of you.
REASON: You promised to help me raise the stones.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: He reaches into his coat, pats the oilskin packet of blue cornflower seeds through the wool, and rests his hand there.
SAY: Doesn't want much, just dry loam on a gentle rise where the sour water won't pool. A plain slab of grey slate at the head.
SAY: And a handful of blue cornflower seeds pressed in come the spring, so the bees know the lease is paid.
REASON: You asked what my own plot would need.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook watches a spark drift up toward the crone's face in the moon, his hands resting flat and still on his knees.
SAY: When you have spent enough winters listening to the earth shift after hours, quiet is the grandest luxury on the books.
SAY: Though I won't deny, sitting round a warm kettle with decent company runs it a very close second.
REASON: You wondered if a quiet grave was enough for me.

TALK devoted
NARRATOR: Rook sets his soggy calfskin ledger and the small oilskin seed packet side by side on his knee, Brushin' ash from the binding.
SAY: Been looking at the road ahead of us, up toward the Wytchwood and that great crooked timber at the heart of it.
SAY: By rights, any sensible municipal clerk would condemn the whole valley for subsidence and post a quarantine notice at the pass.
SAY: You aren't turning back, though, and neither am I. If the docket takes us straight up the Crooked Tree and back down the roots, I'm on the roster.
SAY: You know what I carry in this coat. The ledger with the rubbings, the packet of blue cornflower seeds, and the hope of a quiet plot when the work's done.
SAY: They are the only things keeping my boots pointed toward morning. Everything else went cold in Syndramas a long while back.
SAY: If it comes to a hard corner between this company and my own rest, the ledger can burn and the seeds can scatter in the ditch.
SAY: I left a post once when the roof came down, and I won't leave another. Settle down now, the watch is set.
OPTION 1: We would do the same for you.
OPTION 2: Keep your seeds and your ledger safe.
OPTION 3: Thank you for holding the line with us.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook straps the belt twine round his ledger with a firm, practised tug and looks up at you across the flame.
SAY: I know it, and that is why the shield stays up. Never marched with a platoon that kept better order in the dark.
SAY: Now get your head down while the fire holds. I have the first watch, and the perimeter is quiet.
REASON: You said you would stand by me the same way.
INSPIRE: Swore to hold the line for us.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: He tucks the oilskin packet back inside his lining and pats his chest twice, remembering to draw a slow, steady breath.
SAY: Oh, I intend to bring the paperwork home clean if the ground allows it. A watchman doesn't lose his kit unless the ditch caves in.
SAY: Just wanted the priority logged in advance, so there is no confusion when the masonry starts falling.
REASON: You told me not to give up what I carry.
INSPIRE: Put our lives ahead of his rest.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: The brass knocker on Rook's shield gives one small, settled clink as he shifts his weight to stand guard.
SAY: No need for thanks when a man is only doing the job he signed on for. You lot gave a cold guard a proper post again.
SAY: Get some sleep while the coals are red. Nothing unruly gets past this shield tonight.
REASON: You thanked me for standing watch over the party.
INSPIRE: Pledged his shield and his last rest.
